citeinfo.title: Results from geochemical and mineralogical characterization of Boquillas Shale geochemical reference material ShBOQ-1
Geochemical and mineralogical properties of Boquillas Shale geochemical reference material ShBOQ-1

descript.abstract: This data release accompanies a Fact Sheet on the ShBOQ-1 geochemical reference material (Birdwell and Wilson, 2021). Average and standard deviations reported in the Fact Sheet were calculated using the values compiled here.
descript.purpose: To address industry and research needs for geochemical reference materials relevant to unconventional petroleum resources, particularly source rocks, inorganic chemistry, organic geochemistry, and mineralogy data have been collected on the ShBOQ-1 GRM as part of interlaboratory testing studies. The application emphasis for use of this material is as a calibration or quality control check sample in geochemical surveys of rock geochemistry and mineralogy in petroleum systems.

dataqual.logic: Elemental data: Reporting ranges depend on the element; major elements are reported in weight % and trace elements are reported in parts per million by mass (ppm or mg/kg). Information on reporting ranges and acceptance limits for major and trace metal analysis by ICP-MS/OES is available from the USGS Minerals Resources Program (USGS Minerals Resources Program, 2018). Total organic carbon: Reporting range 0.2 wt. % to 100 wt. %. Programmed pyrolysis (HAWK): Typical reporting ranges for measured values S1, 0-3 mg-hydrocarbon/g-rock S2, 0-40 mg-hydrocarbon/g-rock S3, 0-4 mg-CO2/g-rock Tmax, 300-650°C X-ray diffraction (XRD): Reporting range 0 to 100 wt. %. Extractable organic matter (EOM): Reported in mg-EOM/g-rock and fractions are reported in wt. % of EOM.
dataqual.complete:
Samples were submitted to a contract laboratory through the USGS Minerals Resources Program for analysis of major and trace element chemistry using several USGS Methods incorporating various techniques, including hydride generation atomic absorption spectrometry (HG-AAS), wavelength dispersive X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy (WD-XRF), and inductively coupled plasma (ICP) with mass spectrometry (MS), optical emission spectroscopy (OES), or both. This dataset serves as a supplement but does not supersede results reported as part of the International Association of Geoanalysts GeoPT40A international proficiency test (Webb et al., 2017):
Total Sulfur (Method 2)
Total Carbon (Method 3)
Carbonate Carbon (Method 4)
Mercury by cold vapor atomic absorption spectrometry (Method 5)
Arsenic by HG-AAS (Method 6)
Antimony by HG-AAS (Method 7)
Selenium by HG-AAS (Method 8)
Chloride by ion selective electrode (Method 10)
Ferrous Oxide by acid titration (Method 11)
WD-XRF Major Element (Method 15)
16 ICP-OES major element (Method 16)
42 Element ICP-OES-MS multi-acid near total (Method 17)
55 Element ICP-OES-MS sodium peroxide fusion (Method 18)
Appropriate check standards were included, and concentrations are reported on a whole rock basis (wt. % or ppm, mg/kg).
Samples were analyzed for total organic carbon (TOC) content and programmed pyrolysis parameters as part of interlaboratory testing studies using a variety of instruments and methods depending on the particular laboratory (Birdwell and Wilson, 2017; Birdwell and Wilson, 2019). Some laboratories also included total carbon (TC) content measurements. Generally, carbon and programmed pyrolysis analyses are performed according to the instrument manufacturers’ instructions with internal calibration and laboratory check standards run for quality assurance purposes. TOC analyses made using “LECO-type” instruments (combustion and CO2 detection by infrared spectroscopy) first required removal of carbonate minerals using dilute acid treatment. Information on measured and calculated parameters for programmed pyrolysis can be found in Peters and others (2005) and references therein.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) mineralogy was determined on aliquots of the Boquillas GRM provided to several laboratories as part of interlaboratory testing (Birdwell and Wilson, 2019). Sample preparation, instrumentation, analysis parameters, and diffractogram interpretation varied between laboratories. All mineralogy results are reported on an organic-free basis (wt. %).
Extractable organic matter content of rock samples (~10-40 g) were determined by extraction with chloroform using a Soxhlet apparatus for approximately 48 hours at the USGS Petroleum Geochemistry Research Laboratory in Denver, Colorado using an internal standard operating procedure.

procstep.procdesc:
The material for the Boquillas Shale GRM was collected at a road cut off US-90 west of Del Rio in Val Verde County, Texas, in April 2015 (approx. 720 kg; 29°42'10.0"N, 101°12'40.1"W). Various tools, including sledgehammers, wedges, and smaller pickaxes and hammers were used to remove rock material from the face of the road cut. Material was then stored in sealed 5-gallon plastic buckets for transport to the laboratory.
Upon arrival at the USGS facility in Denver, CO, the sample material was examined for contamination occurring during collection or transport and any contaminants (debris, plant material, etc.) were physically removed. Starting material for the crushed and powdered versions of the GRM were broken up with a standard sledgehammer until the sample size was reduced to less than 15 cm in diameter. This material was then further crushed using a Sturtevant jaw crusher with the crush plate adjusted to a three centimeters gap. The material was fed to the crusher at a rate of twenty kilograms per hour. Following this step, the material was sieved using a Kason 30 cm vibratory screening device equipped with a one centimeter (opening size) stainless steel screen. Material passing the screen was retained and the oversized material re-crushed. The final supply of < 1 cm crushed (chip) material was divided into two equal parts. One aliquot was further processed to obtain the powdered reference material. This aliquot was run through jaw crusher again with the crush plate set to approximately two millimeters. The < 2 mm material was divided into lots of 20 kg (five-gallon containers) and each lot was ground in a 30-gallon ball mill filled with 80 kg of one inch diameter corundum grinding media over a period of at least 12 hours. When the grinding was completed, the powdered material was removed and transferred to plastic lined five gallon buckets.
After crushing and grinding, the chip and powdered aliquots were each homogenized using a 10 ft3 cross flow V-blender. The material was blended for one hour after which it is removed from the blender in five-gallon aliquots. After blending, a two-step splitting process was applied utilizing a USGS designed spinning riffler. The spinning riffler consists of a rotating (2-3 rpm) platform with a set of receiving containers that pass beneath a sample reservoir containing the material to be subdivided. This rotary motion continuously distributes material between all the receiving containers thus minimizing sample segregation. The first splitting utilized a series of stainless steel V-splitters (12), each positioned over a five-gallon bucket. This coarse splitting step divides the entire blended supply into twelve equal (mass) units. A randomly selected subset of these buckets is then selected and subdivided into twelve new buckets. This process is continued until a sample mass of 6120 g is obtained for each coarse split unit. The V-splitters are then removed and the riffler platform reconfigured to hold a 72-position bottling ring. A set of bottles (72, 4-oz) are place in the ring and the sample reservoir filled with a single coarse split unit. The bottles are rotated beneath the reservoir and receive 1-5 grams of material on each rotation. This process continues until the contents of the reservoir are transferred to the bottles. At the end of each run, the bottles are removed, capped, and labeled and another set of bottles are positioned in the ring. The mass of each finished bottle is determined to ensure that a minimum sample mass of 80 grams is achieved. This process is continued until all homogenized material is subdivided into bottles. The same procedure was followed for the “chip” material but with larger (9-oz) bottles used as the containers.

overview.eaover:
Inorganic Chemistry Tab Column A: Bottle number GRM sample was taken from assigned by USGS Geochemical Reference Materials Project. Column B: Arsenic measured by HG-AAS (ppm, mg/kg). Column C: Chloride by ion selective electrode (ppm, mg/kg). Column D: Carbonate carbon (as CO2; wt. %). Column E: Carbonate carbon (as C; wt. %). Column F: Ferrous Oxide by titration (wt. %). Column G: Mercury by cold vapor atomic absorption spectrometry (ppm, mg/kg). Column H: Organic carbon by coulometry (wt. %). Column I: Antimony by HG-AAS (ppm, mg/kg). Column J: Selenium by HG-AAS (ppm, mg/kg). Column K: Tellurium by HG-AAS (ppm, mg/kg). Column L: Total carbon (wt. %). Column M: Total sulfur (wt. %). Columns N through V: 16 element ICP-OES major elements (reported in wt. %). Columns W through AC: 16 element ICP-OES trace elements (reported in ppm, mg/kg). Columns AD through AK: 42 element ICP-OES-MS major elements (reported in wt. %). Columns AL through BS: 42 element ICP-OES-MS minor elements (ppm, mg/kg). Columns BT through CC: 55 element ICP-OES-MS major elements (reported in wt. %). Columns CD through DZ: 55 element ICP-OES-MS minor elements (ppm, mg/kg). Columns EA through EL: WD-XRF major element oxides (wt. %).
Organic Geochemistry tab Column A: Bottle number GRM sample was taken from assigned by USGS Geochemical Reference Materials Project. Column B: Laboratory number assigned to the participant. Column C: TOC determined by participating laboratory (wt. %). Column D: Programmed pyrolysis instrument used by participating laboratory for analysis (Rock Eval 2 by Delsi Inc.; Rock Eval 6 by Vinci Instruments; SRA = Source Rock Analyzer by Weatherford; HAWK = Hydrocarbon Analyzer With Kinetics by Wildcat Technologies). Column E: Weight of sample used in programmed pyrolysis analysis by participating laboratory (mg). Columns F through J: Measured values from programmed pyrolysis (PP), including PP TOC (wt. %), S1 or free hydrocarbons (mg-hydrocarbon/g-rock), S2 or pyrolysis hydrocarbon content (mg-hydrocarbon/g-rock), S3 or organic oxygen content as CO2 (mg-CO2/g-rock), and Tmax or temperature at maximum S2 generation (°C). For more details, see Peters and others, 2005. Columns K through M: Total (K), Mineral (L), or Carbonate (M) carbon reported by participant (wt. %).
Mineralogy Tab Column A: Bottle number GRM sample was taken from assigned by USGS Geochemical Reference Materials Project. Column B: Laboratory number assigned to the participant. Columns C through O: Mineral phases identified by XRD participating laboratories (wt. %). Cells containing “trace” notation indicates mineral was detected but not quantified.
Extractable organic matter Tab Column A: Lab number assigned to USGS Energy Resources Program Petroleum Geochemistry Research Laboratory. Column B: Sample replicate number assigned by the analyst. Column C: Bottle number GRM sample was taken from assigned by USGS Geochemical Reference Materials Project. Column D: Extractable organic matter (EOM) content (mg-EOM/kg-rock). Column E: Extractable organic matter (EOM) content (wt. %).
